name: Beth Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Beth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Okay. I'm Beth, I'm 27, and I manage the orchards at Holm Fruit Farm. That's about 70 hectares of apples and pears, plus a flock of sheep the Holms run under the trees in winter to keep the grass down. I've got four people year-round and around 30 pickers in September.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Winter is pruning, which is the part I'm known for. I can look at a tree and know which branch will fruit in two years and which is wasting its effort. Spring is frost nights, when we're up at two in the morning running the wind machines, and summer is thinning and spraying. Picking is six weeks of madness, checking every bin before it goes to the cold store. I love the quiet of pruning in February. What wears me out is a late frost that takes half the blossom in one night.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's at home, and how do you use AI, if at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Erik, who drives a lorry for the farm merchant. I don't use AI tools at all, not even on my phone. The Holms bought a camera system on the grading line that sorts the apples by size and colour, and that's fine, but I don't need it in the orchard. We've got about two months' money put by, maybe a bit more after picking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. We call this one AI Plateau.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right to me. Most things turn out that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was overblown, like a lot of things. The grading camera is useful, the rest was talk. Trees still need pruning by someone who's done it for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel I'd been right not to bother. I'm not against it, I just didn't see the point of chasing it. I'd be quietly glad nobody's going to ask me to prune with a tablet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Prune the same blocks, run the same team, keep an eye on the frost. Erik and I would put a bit more into savings after a good picking, maybe aim for four months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a frost night where the temperature stops at plus one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything at all change in the orchard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the spray records would be done by the computer. Mrs Holm would like that, she hates the paperwork more than I do. But the pruning, the frost, the picking, no.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd miss out on, if AI fizzled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think so. Maybe better frost warnings, because the forecast is wrong too often. But we manage, we've always managed.

S0.say: I'd say it was overblown, like a lot of things, and the grading camera was the only useful part. Trees still need pruning by someone who's done it for years.
S0.think: Privately I'd feel I'd been right not to bother chasing it. I'm not against it, but I'd be glad nobody asks me to prune with a tablet.
S0.do: Carries on pruning the same blocks and running the same team. Puts more into savings after a good picking with Erik, aiming for four months of expenses.
S0.feel: Calm, like a frost night that stops just above freezing.
S0.quote: I'd be quietly glad nobody's going to ask me to prune with a tablet.
S0.fieldNote: Beth is matter-of-fact and slow to be impressed. She's not against technology, she just doesn't see the point of chasing it. Her pride sits in pruning skill, and the plateau leaves that untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. We call this one Steady Disruption.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. That's harder to dismiss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's see what actually works before anyone rushes out and buys it. Half the kit at farm shows ends up in the back of a shed. I'd be careful, not against it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think picking will go to robots first, and I'd be fine with that, we can never get enough pickers. Pruning would take longer. But I'd worry they'd replant the orchards in flat walls of trees that a machine can prune, and then what's my skill worth?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait at least a season and watch what the big fruit farm down the valley does. If the Holms brought in a picking robot, I'd learn to manage it because I'd have to. I'd keep spending the same and put a bit more by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like seeing your neighbour grub out an old orchard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said flat walls of trees. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some growers already plant the trees close together on wires, so the fruit hangs on a flat wall. It's easier for a machine to see and reach. It works, but it's not pruning as I learned it, it's more like trimming a hedge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the Holms replanted that way, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grumble, then do it properly. I've worked here since I was 19. I'm not going to walk out over the shape of a tree, but I'd want to keep the old block by the house as it is.

S1.say: I'd say let's see what actually works before anyone rushes to buy it, because half the kit at farm shows ends up in a shed. I'd be careful, not against it.
S1.think: Privately I think picking goes to robots first, which I'd welcome. But if they replant in flat walls a machine can prune, I'd wonder what my skill is worth.
S1.do: Waits at least a season to watch what a larger fruit farm nearby does. Learns to manage a picking robot if her employer buys one, keeps spending the same and puts a little more into savings.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with a sense of losing the craft she's proud of.
S1.quote: It works, but it's not pruning as I learned it, it's more like trimming a hedge.
S1.fieldNote: Beth welcomes robots for picking because of labour shortages, but her real concern is the slow loss of a craft. She's pragmatic rather than political and blames nobody. She'd adapt grudgingly and fight only to keep one old block as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. We call this one AGI by 2028.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? I'd want to see that before I believed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'll believe it when I see a robot get through a frost night. In public I'd keep calm, because there's no use getting everyone in a state. People still need to eat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, if it's true, I think the Holms would sell up or put in machines, and I'd be out within a couple of seasons. I don't have anything else, I've done orchards since I left university. That scares me more than I'd say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd cut back. No holiday, no new car, and I'd keep the two months' savings for the gap. I'd ask the Holms straight what they're planning. If the job went, I'd probably help my dad on his smallholding while I worked out what next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Mostly because I wouldn't know what to do instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do instead, if you had to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. Maybe drive a lorry like Erik, but that'd go too in this picture, wouldn't it? I'd be looking for anything outdoors with people, and I don't know what that is yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think there's one person to blame. The Holms would be doing what they had to. The government should have seen it coming, but I'm not sure anyone could have, in two years.

S2.say: I'd say I'll believe it when I see a robot get through a frost night. I'd keep calm in public, because people still need to eat.
S2.think: Privately, if it's true, the Holms would sell or bring in machines and I'd be out within two seasons. I've done nothing but orchards since university, and that scares me.
S2.do: Cuts back at once with no holiday or new car, and protects her two months of savings for a gap. Asks her employers directly about their plans and falls back on helping at her father's smallholding if the job goes.
S2.feel: Anxious, mainly from not knowing what she'd do instead.
S2.quote: Maybe drive a lorry like Erik, but that'd go too in this picture, wouldn't it?
S2.fieldNote: Beth's public calm hides real fear, rooted in having only one trade. She doesn't blame her employers or anyone in particular, which fits her centre outlook. Her fallback is family, her father's smallholding, rather than the state.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. We call this one AGI by 2031.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's five prunings. It's still not very long for trees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is nothing in an orchard, because a new tree takes three years to fruit. Growers should be careful not to rip out good trees for a promise. I'd say that at the growers' meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years means I'd get a few more seasons, then probably the same as the fast one. I'd keep telling myself it might not happen, and I know that's a habit of mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on for the first year or two and save harder, maybe get to four months. I'd watch the farms that buy robots and see how they get on. Around year three, if it looked real, I'd ask the Holms to train me on the new systems so I'm the one running them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not panicking, but not sleeping as well as I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd tell yourself it might not happen. Is that a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Erik says I do it with everything, I left the car's brakes until they were grinding. With five years, I'd probably leave it until year three before doing anything. That's maybe too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you spend your savings on, if not a holiday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing, that's the point. It's for the gap. Maybe a course if I had to, but the Holms should pay for that.

S3.say: I'd say five years is nothing in an orchard, because a new tree takes three years to fruit. Growers shouldn't rip out good trees for a promise.
S3.think: Privately five years buys me a few more seasons and then the same as the fast one. I'd keep telling myself it might not happen, and I know that's a habit of mine.
S3.do: Carries on for a year or two and saves harder, aiming for four months. Watches farms that adopt robots and, around year three, asks her employers to train her to run the new systems.
S3.feel: Uneasy and sleeping a little worse, but not panicking.
S3.quote: Erik says I do it with everything, I left the car's brakes until they were grinding.
S3.fieldNote: Beth sees time in tree years: five years is barely a planting cycle. She's honest that she'd delay acting, with a homely example about her car's brakes. Her plan is to become the one who runs the machines, but only once it's clearly real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. We call this one AGI by 2036.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's long enough to plant an orchard and see it crop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do it sensibly, without ripping everything out at once. Growers should keep the old varieties and the people who know them. I'd be saying plan it, don't panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think I've got most of a career left in the trees, and that's a relief. At 37 I could still learn something else, I suppose. I'd rather not, but I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on for the first few years. Put money by each picking season. Maybe around year five I'd look at whether Erik and I could buy a small orchard of our own, old trees, selling to the farm shops and cider makers, the kind of place robots wouldn't bother with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It's far enough off that I can still plan around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A small orchard of your own. Would that work if AGI arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Maybe people would still pay a bit more for apples from a person they know. Or maybe not, and then I've got a nice orchard and no living. It's a risk, but at least it'd be mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you have to save for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot more than two months, that's for sure. A deposit on land would take most of the ten years. Maybe the Holms would sell us the old block by the house, if they went over to machines.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to do it sensibly without ripping everything out at once. Keep the old varieties and the people who know them, plan it and don't panic.
S4.think: Privately, I've got most of a career left in the trees, and that's a relief. At 37 I could still learn something else, though I'd rather not.
S4.do: Carries on and saves after each picking season. Around year five, looks at buying a small orchard of old trees with Erik, perhaps the old block from her employers, to sell to farm shops and cider makers.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with room to plan.
S4.quote: Maybe people would still pay a bit more for apples from a person they know.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Beth think in orchard time, and her plan becomes owning a small, old-style orchard. She's honest that it may not pay. Her caution remains, but the long runway lets her slow habits fit.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd have nothing to move to and no time to find it. What would help is being trained on whatever comes, paid by the farm, and a bit of time to keep the old trees going while it all settles.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the trees themselves. Some of our pear trees are 60 years old. Whatever happens to me, I'd want somebody to look after them properly.

headlineQuote: Maybe people would still pay a bit more for apples from a person they know.
portrait: Beth is a 27-year-old orchard manager on a 70-hectare apple and pear farm, known for her pruning and living with Erik, a lorry driver. She's pragmatic, blames nobody in particular, and never uses AI tools. She waits, watches what other farms do and admits she tends to leave things too late. The fast scenario frightens her because orchards are her only trade, while ten years lets her plan in tree time, even towards a small orchard of her own.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she'd have nothing to move to and no time to find it.
whatWouldHelp: Farm-paid training on the new systems, and time to keep the old trees going while things settle.
